title: Cropland Redistribution: A Synergistic Strategy for Boosting Grain Production While Mitigating Soil Erosion
content:
Abstract

China faces significant spatial mismatches between steeply sloped cropland and gently sloped forest and orchard land. Optimizing the spatial distribution of cropland is critical for food security and ecological conservation in China, where cropland resources are scarce. This study employed the MaxEnt model to evaluate cropland suitability under population and climate change scenarios and conducted a cropland redistribution based on suitability. It evaluated the multifaceted effects of redistribution in terms of slope, suitability, fragmentation, grain production, and soil erosion. The results show that land suitable for cropland in China, categorized as highly suitable, moderately suitable, marginally suitable, conditionally suitable, and unsuitable, accounts for 15.39%, 10.37%, 10.09%, 13.23%, and 50.92% of the total area, respectively. China has substantial potential for cropland redistribution, with approximately 18% of cropland eligible for redistribution, primarily concentrated in the Inner Mongolia and the Great Wall region, Loess Plateau region, Southwest region, South China region, and Middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River region. Cropland redistribution offers multiple benefits, including reducing cropland fragmentation, enhancing habitat integrity, decreasing cropland slope by 16.04% (0.9°), and increasing cropland suitability levels by 7.14% (0.048). Notably, it can boost grain production by 3.10% (approximately 22 Mt), supporting an additional 55 million people, while reducing soil erosion by approximately 21.82% (3.19 t·ha−1·a−1). Designing effective land use policies, such as implementing regional comprehensive land consolidation, establishing a compensation mechanism for farmers' losses, restructuring farmers' land property rights, and improving land management and planning, can facilitate the implementation of cropland redistribution.
